title: Workstream 3 (promote rules into the default artifact) is deferred pending a sized measurement round
description:
Artifact resolution workstreams 1 and 2 shipped (PR #310). Workstream 3 -- promoting the model-agnostic rules from the variants into defaultExtractionArtifact -- is deliberately not done. It is gated on a measurement round the repo cannot run without an API key, and the analysis below changed what that round has to look like.

Re-grounding against the actual prompt files found the spec's workstream 3 table does not describe what is in the variants. Corrections are recorded in docs/specs/artifact-resolution-in-production.spec.md under Implementation notes; the load-bearing ones:

1. Five of the six named rules exist only in haiku45-2. Only frequency siding is in both variants. Promoting them is not consolidating agreed rules; it is applying Haiku-derived text to every tier, including ones with no variant at all.

2. The spec omits five bullets that ARE byte-identical in both variants (the populations rewrite, complete-instances, enum-is-a-value-constraint, conflict-flags-ambiguity, and the "populations are optional" critical rule). By the spec's own logic those are the strongest promotion candidates.

3. The Open decision "sonnet5 retains objectification and ring guidance" is wrong. sonnet5-3 differs from the default in exactly two lines, neither about objectification or rings. Promoting the union would leave both variants empty -- the real question is whether they get retired, not whether they stay thin.

Decision held by the user pending a run with more rounds. See barwise-814 for the harness work that makes such a run interpretable.
notes:
Re-grounded 2026-08-22 now that barwise-814 has shipped. Three findings change what the round should be, and one changes whether the comparative round is needed at all. Recorded in docs/specs/artifact-resolution-in-production.spec.md under 'Workstream 3, revisited'.

1. The motivating gap is not resolvable and has shrunk. The spec cites 0.760 vs 0.948 (gap 0.188). Two recorded rounds of the same comparison: n=3 gave 0.725 vs 0.828 (gap 0.103); n=5 gave 0.783 vs 0.855 (gap 0.072) against a 95% threshold of 0.090 -- z=1.56, p=0.12. The variant leads in both rounds and in neither by a resolvable margin. Resolving 0.03 needs n=45/config (~644 calls); 0.02 needs n=102 (~1442).

2. Three of the nine promotable lines target failures deterministic code now prevents: frequency min>=1 (conformance 5b, barwise-830) now costs 0.02 not 0.1; populations-satisfy-mandatory (sample:true, barwise-827) is moot for the mandatory half; enumerated-list-is-a-value-constraint is HALF absorbed -- conformance check 3 removes a population duplicating a value constraint already emitted, but nothing converts a population into one when none was emitted, so the prompt keeps that half.

3. A comparative test of means is the wrong instrument. Scoring the seven recorded answer keys is free and deterministic: all seven come back full-rubric with ZERO validation errors and ZERO validation warnings, 1-3 conformance corrections each being the entire penalty. So every warning a live run incurs is addressable, warningsByRule names the rule, and each candidate maps to a named rule (completeness/fact-type-without-uniqueness for the uniqueness bullet, structural/binary-missing-inverse-reading for the both-readings bullet, both warnings at 0.05). One diagnostic run of the DEFAULT over both splits -- 10 cases x 5 = 50 calls -- prices each candidate at 0.05 x its count and says which bullet to promote. The 644-call comparative round returns one blended number that cannot tell them apart.

Recommended order: barwise-835 (make the per-instance role-completeness check deterministic; no API calls to test), then the 50-call diagnostic round against the default, then promote only the lines whose rule actually fires. Still gated on the user authorizing the paid run.

title: promptlab: report per-case SD and the suite standard error so an eval run says whether n was enough
description:
runSuite records every sample but reports only means, so a run cannot tell you whether a difference it shows is real. Working the recorded runs by hand shows why that matters.

Analytic SE of the suite mean reproduces the run-to-run swing we observed empirically:
  haiku45-2, n=5:  SE 0.0318  -> two configs must differ by >0.088 to be distinguishable at 95%
  sonnet5-2, n=3:  SE 0.0398  -> >0.110

Those thresholds are larger than every gap we have used to rank configurations, which is why n=3 could not rank them.

The sharper finding: the noise is one sample, not a spread. A single collapsed sample out of 35 carries 77% of all variance in the Haiku run (project-staffing, 0.000 among 0.98s); a single one of 21 carries 99% in the Sonnet run (university-enrollment, 0.167 among 1.000s). The suite mean is mostly an estimator of whether a collapse happened, not of prompt quality. Splitting collapse rate from quality-given-no-collapse tightens the Sonnet SE 13x, and drops the n needed to resolve a 0.02 regression from ~190 to single digits.

Proposed, smallest first:
- Per-case sample SD and a suite-level standard error on SuiteReport, carried into the history entry. Pure arithmetic over samples already collected; no new calls.
- Print the resolution alongside the mean, e.g. "mean 0.916 +/- 0.062 (95%, n=5)", so a reader cannot quote a mean without its error bar.
- A decision rule in the report: a difference below 2x SE(difference) is inconclusive, stated as such rather than left to the reader.
- Separately (needs a spec, involves a judgment call about the threshold): report collapse count per case, so the bimodal failure is counted rather than averaged away.

Wanted before the next sized run, since it is what makes that run self-diagnosing.

Closed by PR #313. runSuite folds per-case sample SD and the suite standard error through src/stats/dispersion.ts; the CLI prints the 95% margin beside every mean including in `prompt history`, where old rows show '+/- ?'. Below two samples the SD is undefined rather than 0. The collapse-rate split stays deferred -- it needs a threshold, which is a judgment call wanting its own spec.

title: Observability for the LLM surfaces: nothing that costs money is currently visible after the fact
description:
Placeholder for a spec, not a design. Filed while working barwise-814, because the same gap kept showing up: the system collects the signals and then drops them.

What is already measured and then thrown away:
- CompletionResponse carries usage.promptTokens, usage.completionTokens, and latencyMs. Every provider populates them. processTranscript passes them into DraftModelResult. No surface persists them -- not the CLI, not MCP, not VS Code. So there is no answer to "what did that extraction cost" or "how slow is Haiku on a 16KB transcript" without instrumenting a run by hand.
- runSuite records `attempts` per run and the retry classification (FailureKind), which is the only place a rate-limit storm is visible, and it survives only until the process exits.
- The score history is the one durable record, and it holds means and nothing operational.

Questions a spec should answer:
- What is worth persisting, and where? The score history is per-eval-run and checked into git; operational telemetry is per-call and should probably not be.
- Does this belong in a package, or is it a CLI/MCP concern? Determinism-in-core says the collection point is the outer packages, since it is all clocks, counters, and I/O.
- Is there a single envelope that serves eval runs, production extractions, and the optimizer lane, or are those three different records that should not be forced together?
- Cost needs per-model pricing, which is external data that goes stale. Record tokens and derive cost at read time rather than baking a number into a row.

Relates to task #2 (model-tier economics), which cannot be answered without the token and latency numbers this would keep.

Spec written as docs/specs/llm-call-observability.spec.md; workstream 1 (the record type and the withCallLog decorator) is implemented. Left open: the CLI sink (W2) and the usage report (W3), both gated on open decisions a reviewer should settle first -- chiefly whether recording is opt-in.

Answers to the questions this issue posed:

- What to persist, and where: one record per completion -- model, tokens in and out, latency, outcome, error class -- as JSONL under $XDG_STATE_HOME/barwise/, matching where the gym already writes. Not in the repo: this is operational data with a different lifetime than promptlab's committed score history.
- Package or surface concern: the recording seam is the LlmClient itself, via a decorator in @barwise/llm. The persistence is the caller's, following the same seam the no-clocks rule and the build provenance already use. processTranscript, reviewModel, and runSuite are all untouched, which is the test of whether the seam is right.
- One envelope or three: one. Eval runs, extractions, and the optimizer lane differ in how calls are grouped, not in what is measured. An optional correlation id is the whole difference.
- Cost: record tokens, never a price. The repo ships no rate table, since a stale price produces a confidently wrong number; a usage report takes --rates from the user.

One constraint the issue did not raise and the spec makes explicit: records carry sizes and identities, never prompt or response text, and errorKind is a classification rather than the provider's message. Transcripts are client material, and a telemetry log quietly accumulating them would be that mistake written to disk. Two tests assert it.
notes:
2026-08-22: workstream 3 SHIPPED -- `barwise llm-usage` reads the log and reports per model: calls, failures by kind, token totals, median and p95 latency. All three workstreams now done; task #2 (model-tier economics) is answerable rather than merely unblocked.

No prices ship with the repo, per the open decision: --rates <file> takes a user-maintained JSON of per-million rates. A checked-in table with a 'last verified' date is friendlier for one release and misleading for every release after.

Percentiles rather than a mean, because a mean hides the tail and the tail is what a timeout is set against; undefined rather than 0 for an empty sample, the same distinction the dispersion module makes. The reader tolerates the file it actually gets: one log holds three record kinds and an append-only file can end mid-line, so non-call records are skipped on a field only a call carries and an unparseable line is skipped rather than fatal.

Still deferred: promptHash on the record (hashPrompt lives in promptlab, which depends on llm and not the reverse; the honest fix is moving the hasher into llm rather than duplicating it).

title: Consider folding Ousterhout's design vocabulary into the architecture guidance
description:
A Philosophy of Software Design covers ground our design principles gesture at without naming, and the vocabulary is worth having because it makes a review comment land in one word instead of a paragraph.

Where it would attach. CLAUDE.md states orthogonality and composability as primary, DRY as secondary, and explicit-over-implicit throughout. Ousterhout's frame is compatible but sharper in places we actually argue:

- Deep vs shallow modules. Our composability principle says "narrow primitives that compose over wide ones that don't", which is the same claim, but "deep module" names the target directly: a simple interface over substantial functionality. The FormatDescriptor registry and resolveArtifact are deep; a wrapper that renames three parameters is shallow. Useful for judging whether a proposed seam earns its place.
- Complexity is what the *reader* pays. Change amplification, cognitive load, unknown unknowns. The third is exactly the failure the artifact-resolution spec kept hitting: nothing told a reader that the variant files had converged, or that the eval harness could not resolve the gaps it was being used to rank.
- Define errors out of existence. Related to explicit-over-implicit but pointed the other way -- rather than requiring the caller to declare, remove the condition. Worth stating alongside, since taken alone "explicit over implicit" can argue for pushing work onto callers, and that is how a shallow interface gets justified.
- Comments describe things the code cannot. Our comment convention is house style by imitation; the "what the code cannot say" test is a real criterion.
- Strategic vs tactical programming, and design-it-twice. Design-it-twice is close to what the spec-writer skill's sensemaking step already asks for (hold two or three alternatives); naming the source would tie them together.

Where it would live: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, or a short section in CLAUDE.md's Design Principles that cites the terms without restating the book. Prefer the smaller edit -- the value is a shared vocabulary, not a summary. A reader who wants the argument should be pointed at the book.

Worth deciding explicitly whether this becomes normative (a reviewer may reject a change for being a shallow module) or descriptive (shared words, no new gate). Recommend descriptive first.

Closed. Landed as a "Shared vocabulary (Ousterhout)" subsection under Design Principles in the root CLAUDE.md, kept descriptive per the recommendation: the terms give a reviewer shorter words, they do not add a gate.

Five terms, each anchored to something already in this codebase rather than restated from the book: deep vs shallow modules (resolveArtifact and the FormatDescriptor registry as the deep cases), the three forms of complexity (with unknown-unknowns named as the one the last two specs kept hitting), define-errors-out-of-existence (explicitly as a counterweight to explicit-over-implicit, which taken alone argues for pushing work onto callers), comments-describe-what-code-cannot, and strategic-over-tactical with design-it-twice tied to the spec-writer skill's sensemaking step.

Placed in CLAUDE.md rather than ARCHITECTURE.md section 8, which holds decisions about this system rather than general design vocabulary, and because CLAUDE.md is what an agent actually reads before working.

title: splitModel's auction test is a latent CI flake: 480ms alone, 5714ms under coverage
description:
tests/project/splitModel.test.ts "splits the auction model into a valid four-domain project" ran 5714ms during a full `npm run test:coverage` and failed on vitest's 5000ms default timeout. The same test standalone takes 480ms. Coverage instrumentation plus twelve packages running in parallel is the difference.

Not reproduced in CI -- the run on PR #313 was green -- which is exactly what makes it worth filing rather than waiting for. It surfaced on a loaded container, so it is a question of runner speed, and a slower or busier runner will hit it.

This is the second instance of the class. The first was loadSuite's seed-suite test in promptlab, fixed by giving that one test an explicit `}, 30_000)`. Same fix applies here.

Worth deciding whether to keep patching per test or raise testTimeout once in the shared vitest config. Per-test is more honest about which tests are genuinely slow; a global default hides that a test got slower. Recommend per-test, consistent with the loadSuite precedent.

Trap for whoever picks this up: `npm run test` and `npm run test:coverage` are different Turborepo tasks, and only the second is what CI runs. A local `npm run test` will not reproduce this.

Closed. The recommendation recorded above -- patch per test, following the loadSuite precedent -- was wrong, and checking the repo rather than generalizing from one remembered instance is what corrected it.

Five packages already set `testTimeout: 30_000` globally in vitest.config.ts (cli, diagram, diagram-ui, llm, mcp), with comments giving exactly this reason: "the 5s default is too tight on a loaded CI runner", "under coverage instrumentation". The per-test patch in promptlab was the anomaly, not the convention.

The cohort is also larger than one test. Under coverage with twelve packages in parallel, core alone has five splitModel tests between 2.8s and 11s, and diagram, llm, and cli each have tests over 5s that pass only because those packages already carry the global. Patching per test would have meant re-deriving this finding on every loaded runner.

The argument that per-test is "more honest about which tests are slow" also does not survive contact: a timeout is a failure threshold, and it fires on machine load rather than on a test getting slower. Vitest already reports per-test durations, which is how the cohort was found. Using the timeout as a slowness alarm is a misuse of it.

Fixed by giving the seven packages that lacked it the same `testTimeout: 30_000` the other five had, so all twelve now agree, and removing promptlab's now-redundant per-test override. Verified load-bearing: lowering core's to 300ms fails five tests, restoring it passes all twelve packages under test:coverage.

title: Truncated LLM responses were scored as prompt failures, not excluded
description:
The first run against the dev split produced three consecutive near-zero scores on vendor-onboarding (0.000, 0.000, 0.133) that were not bad extractions at all. They were complete extractions cut off at the provider's 8,192-token output default, and nothing in the response said so.

Three dev transcripts are 13-17 KB against the seed suite's 1.0-1.6 KB. At the densest observed payload/transcript ratio (9.69, from the seven recorded fixtures) they need 31,700 to 41,600 output tokens. Every one was two to five times over budget.

The failure was invisible because a truncated tool_use block still parses: it arrives as well-formed JSON holding whatever fields completed, so it raised no error and nothing marked it unscorable. It simply scored near zero, which reads exactly like a bad prompt. Both SDKs report this (Anthropic stop_reason=max_tokens, OpenAI finish_reason=length) and the code discarded it.

Same category error as barwise-806, which stopped scoring failed calls as zeroes, and worse for being silent: a failed call at least reports an error.

Fixed per docs/specs/output-budget.spec.md. CompletionRequest.maxTokens overrides the client default per call; CompletionResponse carries stopReason and truncated; suggestMaxTokens derives a budget from transcript length, floored at the client default so every seed case and every recorded history row stays comparable; runSuite excludes truncated runs as failureKind 'truncated' and reports truncations apart from failures; barwise prompt eval gains --max-tokens. processTranscript derives the same budget and surfaces truncation as its first warning rather than shipping half a model silently.

title: MAX_OUTPUT_TOKEN_CAP of 64,000 exceeds some models' own output limits
description:
suggestMaxTokens caps a derived budget at 64,000, sized so the largest transcript in the eval suite (vendor-onboarding, ~41,600 derived tokens) fits. A cap below that would leave the very cases that motivated barwise-818 silently truncated.

The consequence, accepted deliberately and recorded here so it is not rediscovered: a model whose own output ceiling is lower rejects the request outright. gpt-4o allows 16,384. That is a 400 carrying a status, an error type, and a request id, all three now recorded by runSuite, and the remedy is --max-tokens (or ProcessorOptions.maxTokens). Being told a budget is impossible beats being handed a fragment that scores like a bad prompt.

Not fixed with a per-model table on purpose: the SDKs do not expose each model's output limit, and a hand-maintained table would go stale without anything noticing. Revisit only if a real user hits this on a default path, in which case the fix is probably for the provider to clamp and report the clamp, never to clamp silently.

title: Consider a transcript cleanup pass before ORM extraction
description:
Idea from the user (2026-08-22): a lightweight pass over a raw transcript before it reaches the extraction prompt -- strip timestamps, speaker noise, filler, verbatim repetition -- so the model sees signal rather than transport.

Worth noting up front that this sounds easier than it is, which is the user's own framing. Two hazards specific to barwise:

1. Provenance. Every extracted element carries a SourceReference with line numbers and excerpts into the original transcript. A cleanup pass that renumbers lines breaks that unless it emits a line map back to the original, which is most of the work.
2. Determinism. If cleanup is deterministic it belongs in core and is testable; if it is an LLM pass it doubles the calls and adds a second source of non-determinism upstream of the metric, which would make eval scores harder to attribute, not easier.

The measurable upside is real and now quantifiable: the dev transcripts are 13-17 KB against 1.0-1.6 KB for the seed cases, and input size drives both cost and the output budget (barwise-818). A deterministic pass that halved transcript size would halve both.

Needs a spec before any code. The eval harness is the right place to settle it: score the same cases with and without cleanup and see whether it moves the mean beyond the suite's resolvable difference. If it does not, it is cost reduction only, which is still a result worth having but a different justification.

title: Anthropic SDK refuses non-streaming calls above 21,333 max_tokens
description:
Fallout from barwise-818, found on the first dev-split run after it landed. All three cases came back FAILED, excluded with: 'Streaming is strongly recommended for operations that may token longer than 10 minutes.'

@anthropic-ai/sdk 0.52.0 calculateNonstreamingTimeout throws when (3_600_000 * max_tokens) / 128_000 exceeds the 600_000ms default, i.e. for any max_tokens above 21,333. It throws before the request is sent, and no timeout argument escapes it in this version. The derived budget for a 17 KB transcript is roughly 41,600, so every dev case tripped it.

The retry classifier handled it correctly, for what it is worth: terminal, 1 attempt, no wasted backoff.

Fixed by streaming unconditionally in AnthropicLlmClient and taking finalMessage(). Not for incremental display -- nothing renders these tokens -- but so no call can reach the guard at all. Streaming only above a threshold was rejected: the threshold is a constant inside someone else's package and can move without warning, which is the failure mode this whole line of work keeps hitting. finalMessage() reassembles input_json_deltas into a complete tool_use block, so the rest of the provider sees exactly what the non-streaming call returned, partial input included.

Note the mock cannot prove the SDK's real streaming behaviour; the live dev-split run is the proof.

title: Cache the extraction prompt prefix instead of resending 5,780 tokens per call
description:
Measured while sizing the output budget: every extraction call sends a byte-identical 5,780-token preamble before a line of transcript -- 4,540 for the system prompt, 1,180 for the response schema (which reaches the wire as the extraction tool's input_schema), 58 scaffold. For the seven seed cases the transcript is 6% of what we send; the rest is our own prompt. A repeat=5 sweep over ten cases sends that preamble fifty times: 289,000 input tokens of pure repetition.

Fixed per docs/specs/prompt-caching.spec.md. CompletionRequest gains cacheSystemPrompt and cacheUserMessage; the Anthropic provider marks the corresponding blocks with cache_control. Two flags rather than one because their break-even conditions differ: a write costs ~1.25x and a read ~0.1x, so the preamble is worth caching whenever a run makes two or more calls, while a transcript is only worth caching when the same case is sampled again (runSuite iterates case-outer, repeat-inner, so repeats send identical transcripts back to back).

Note the layout was already correct by accident: the API renders tools then system then messages, and the extraction call happens to put its stable content first. Nothing said so, so a later change moving the transcript earlier or interpolating a date into the system prompt would have cost the whole saving with no test failing. The ordering is now a stated invariant in the package CLAUDE.md.

title: Report cache hits in the eval output, so caching is confirmed rather than assumed
description:
barwise-822 turns caching on for eval sweeps but nothing reports whether it worked. The failure mode is silent by construction: below a model's minimum cacheable length, or after any byte change in the prefix, cache_creation_input_tokens is simply 0 and the request succeeds normally. The only symptom is a bill.

CompletionResponse.usage carries promptTokens and completionTokens but has no field for cache_creation_input_tokens or cache_read_input_tokens. Adding them means touching the usage shape and every provider that fills it, which is why it was cut from the caching change rather than bundled in.

Worth noting that input_tokens is the UNCACHED REMAINDER once caching is on -- total prompt size is input_tokens + cache_creation + cache_read. Any future cost reporting that reads promptTokens alone will under-report by the cached portion, which is most of it.

RESOLVED per docs/specs/cache-reporting.spec.md. CompletionResponse.usage gains cacheReadTokens and cacheWriteTokens, populated by Anthropic (both counters) and OpenAI (reads only -- its caching is automatic and server-side, so there is no client-controlled write). SuiteReport.cache totals them, the verbose line shows reads live, and the CLI warns when caching was requested, more than one call was made, and nothing was read back.

Absent and zero are kept distinct throughout: a provider with no cache says nothing and gets no row; a provider that cached nothing says zero and gets one, because zero across a repeated prefix is the fault worth naming.

HistoryEntry.tokens carries prompt/completion/cacheRead/cacheWrite. Scoped deliberately: unlike every other field in a row these say nothing about comparability (caching is score-neutral), but cost is a longitudinal question and four numbers let a later reader reconstruct it against whatever price table exists then. Stop reasons, request ids and HTTP statuses stay off the record -- they diagnose a run that is happening, and are useless three weeks later.

title: Investigate prompt caching as a default for interactive barwise usage
description:
From the user (2026-08-22): whenever the llm package is used, defaulting to cached prompts could save real money on interactive sessions.

barwise-822 deliberately scoped caching to the eval lane, on the reasoning that a one-shot processTranscript reads the cache zero times and pays the 1.25x write for nothing. That reasoning does not survive contact with interactive use, which is the point being made here: a VS Code chat session, an MCP client working through a model, or a user importing several transcripts in a sitting all make repeated calls inside the 5-minute TTL, and every one of them re-sends the same 5,780-token preamble at full price.

What needs establishing before changing a default:

1. Call frequency per surface. The break-even is two calls within the TTL. VS Code chat almost certainly clears it; a single CLI import almost certainly does not; MCP is unknown and depends on the client.
2. Whether the preamble is actually identical across those calls. review and extraction are different surfaces with different prompts, so they are different cache entries; a session alternating between them may thrash rather than accumulate.
3. Whether the default should be per-surface rather than global. Extraction repeats within a session more plausibly than review does.

Depends on barwise-823: without cache-hit reporting there is no way to confirm a default is working rather than quietly costing 25% more on every first call. Do that first.

title: Ollama provider: use native /api/chat so the context window is settable
description:
The Ollama provider talked to the OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoint, which cannot set num_ctx. Ollama's own docs say so: 'The OpenAI API does not have a way of setting the context size for a model', with a Modelfile or a server-wide OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH as the documented workarounds -- neither reachable from a library.

That is disqualifying rather than inconvenient. Ollama defaults to a 4,096-token context and silently drops what does not fit; the extraction system prompt alone is ~4,540 tokens (barwise-822 measured it). On the default, the INSTRUCTIONS are truncated before the transcript is read, and the model is then scored on a prompt it never saw. Same class of silent corruption as barwise-818, entering through a different door.

Rewritten against native /api/chat over fetch. Gains options.num_ctx and options.num_predict, and native `format` which takes a JSON schema directly rather than the response_format/json_schema wrapper. Adds no dependency -- fetch is Node core -- so this provider now uses no SDK at all. suggestContextWindow derives a window per call from prompt length plus output budget; OllamaClientOptions.contextWindow overrides, reachable as `barwise prompt eval --context-window`.

Correction worth recording, because it was stated wrongly mid-investigation: the compat layer DOES report truncation. It passes done_reason through to finish_reason unchanged, and Ollama's vocabulary matches OpenAI's ('length' on num_predict or context exhaustion). The earlier claim that Ollama truncation was undetectable was wrong; describeOpenAiStop already handled it. num_ctx alone justifies the move.

Streams, like the Anthropic provider and more acutely: a local model generating tens of thousands of tokens runs for many minutes, and a non-streaming request sends no headers until it finishes -- past Node's 300s header timeout. The NDJSON reader buffers partial lines.

title: Conformance passed single-role disjunctive constraints the validator rejects
description:
Found by the first dev-split run that completed without truncation. No case was truncated -- every one finished well inside its budget (12,604/41,640; 14,177/35,255; 10,509/31,700) -- so the remaining failures were ours.

isValidArity in ExtractionConformance fell through to a permissive '>= 1' for disjunctive_mandatory, exclusion and exclusive_or, while core's constraintConsistency rule rejects exactly those three below 2 roles. Conformance waved them through and the validator errored on every one, at 0.1 penalty each.

incident-response scored 0.000 on seven such errors; subscription-billing lost 0.1 to one. Neither module was wrong on its own terms, which is why nothing caught it: they are separate by design but not independent, since conformance exists to hand the parser something the validator will accept.

Fixed by listing the three types explicitly at '>= 2', matching the validator. Removal rather than repair: a single-role disjunction is a contradiction in terms, and converting it to a plain mandatory constraint would assert a rule the extraction never stated -- which is precisely what produced vendor-onboarding's separate failure (barwise-827). Removal also charges 0.02 as a conformance correction instead of 0.1 as a validation error, which is the right relative price.

The regression test asserts the agreement end to end rather than the removal alone: a module-local test would re-pin one side of a disagreement and a future relaxation of either module would pass it while re-creating the bug. Verified load-bearing -- reverting the fix fails 7 of 10.

title: Extraction asserts mandatory constraints its own populations violate
description:
vendor-onboarding scored 0.023 on the dev split with: 'Mandatory constraint on role ... in fact type "Vendor has VendorStatus" is violated: "Meridian Components" appears in the model but does not play this mandatory role.'

The same extraction supplied both halves: an inferred mandatory constraint, and a population instance that does not satisfy it. Distinct from barwise-826 -- that was two modules disagreeing; this is one extraction contradicting itself.

enforceConformance can see both halves, so it is the natural place to reconcile them. Three options, none obviously right, which is why this is filed rather than fixed:

1. Drop the mandatory constraint. Safe, loses a rule the transcript may genuinely support.
2. Drop the offending population instance. Keeps the rule, discards evidence -- and populations are what make a model checkable.
3. Leave both and let it be a validation error. Status quo, and arguably honest: the model really is inconsistent and a human should look.

Worth settling with data rather than argument: check how often the pattern occurs across the recorded payloads before choosing. If it is common, option 1 or 2 is worth the loss; if rare, the status quo is a correct signal, not a defect.

Note the prompt angle too: a mandatory constraint over a role no instance plays may indicate the extraction inferred mandatory from a sample rather than from a stated rule.

RESOLVED per docs/specs/sample-populations.spec.md, and none of the three options above was right. The defect was not that the extraction contradicts itself -- it was that nothing in the model said its populations are samples, so the validator assumed the stricter reading. Population gains a `sample` flag (default false, so every existing model is unchanged); sample instances are excluded from the object universe and still counted in valuesPlayedInRole. A sample is positive evidence only: it can satisfy a constraint, never raise the obligation that one be satisfied.

The data settled it: all seven seed answer keys produce zero population-rule errors, so the pattern does not exist in the train split. It is a scaling artifact of realistic-length transcripts, and it reached the product too -- anyone importing a long transcript in the editor saw the same violations.

title: Investigate data profiling to derive domain understanding
description:
Idea from the user (2026-08-22): profile actual data to derive domain understanding, rather than relying only on transcripts.

Fits barwise's existing shape better than it might first appear. The metamodel already has the target concept -- Population -- and as of barwise-827 it distinguishes a significant population (complete, checkable as a closed world) from a sample. Profiled data is the first source that could legitimately produce SIGNIFICANT populations: unlike a transcript, a table really does contain every row.

That matters more than it sounds. Constraint discovery from data is exactly the closed-world inference the population rules already implement, run backwards: a column with no nulls suggests a mandatory role; a column with unique values suggests a uniqueness constraint; a bounded value set suggests a value constraint; a foreign key suggests a fact type. The validation engine can then check the inferred constraints against the same data that suggested them.

Open questions before any spec:

1. Where does it live? Profiling reads data sources, which is I/O -- so a connector package on the @barwise/code-analysis or @barwise/dbt model, not core. The inference itself is deterministic and could be core.
2. What sources? A dbt project already declares models and tests; the dbt connector may already reach most of what is needed without a database connection.
3. How does it combine with transcript extraction? A transcript gives intent and naming; data gives structure and actual distributions. Merging the two is where the value is, and diffModels already exists to compare them -- a data-derived model diffed against a transcript-derived one would surface exactly the disagreements worth a human's attention.

Worth noting the sequencing: it is more valuable AFTER the extraction quality work settles, because it gives a second, independent signal to check extraction against.

title: Output budget floor of 8,192 truncated a small train case; output does not track input size
description:
The first clean train sweep truncated university-enrollment at exactly 8,192 output tokens. Its transcript is 1,486 bytes -- the THIRD largest of the seven train cases, not the largest -- and its recorded answer key is only ~3,500 tokens. Live extraction generated more than twice that.

Measured across the whole suite, live output vs transcript size:

  1.0-1.6 KB transcripts -> 3.7k to 8.2k+ output (implied ratio 12 to 22+)
  13.1-17.2 KB transcripts -> 12.2k to 14.4k output (implied ratio 3 to 4)

Output barely moves across a seventeen-fold range of input. Two nearly identical train transcripts (1,589 B and 1,529 B) produced 7,220 and 4,735 tokens. Output is governed by how much MODEL the domain implies, not by how many bytes it took to describe -- university enrollment is a rich domain expressed briefly.

So the proportional-to-input model from barwise-818 is the wrong SHAPE, not merely mis-tuned, and it is wrongest at the small end where the required ratio is highest -- precisely where it was assumed safest.

Fixed by splitting MIN_DERIVED_OUTPUT_TOKENS (16,384) from DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS (8,192, still the provider default for a call that names no budget). The floor sits 14% above the largest output observed anywhere (14,393, subscription-billing).

Note the old floor's justification was 'a case that fit before must behave exactly as it did', to preserve comparability with recorded history. That was empty: main had no recorded history at all (the rows live on optimization-evals-3 and predate barwise-826/827). The comparability argument was protecting nothing while the truncation was real.

title: Conformance did not check frequency bounds the validator rejects
description:
Third instance of the barwise-826 pattern, found on the first clean train sweep: clinic-appointments lost 0.1 to 'Frequency constraint in fact type "Appointment has FollowUpNote" has min 0, which must be at least 1.'

InferredConstraint carries min and max for frequency constraints. constraintConsistency rejects min < 1 and a max below its min. enforceConformance checked ARITY for frequency constraints but never the bounds, so a min-0 frequency sailed through and became an unavoidable validation error at 0.1.

barwise-826 fixed this class for arity and its own test comment stated the general rule -- 'any rule the validator enforces on arity has to be enforced here too' -- but the fix was scoped to arity when the principle is broader. Worth remembering: the fix landed with a comment that described the general case and code that handled one instance of it.

Fixed with an invalid_bounds correction, removing rather than repairing: a frequency of 'at least 0' is not a weak constraint but no constraint at all -- every population satisfies it -- so nothing a reader could have relied on is lost. Same end-to-end invariant test as barwise-826: whatever survives conformance must not trip the validator.

Follow-up worth doing deliberately rather than reactively: audit constraintConsistency for any REMAINING structural rule conformance does not mirror, instead of waiting for the next eval run to find the fourth instance.

title: Audit constraintConsistency for structural rules conformance does not mirror
description:
Three times now a validator rule with no conformance counterpart has surfaced as an unavoidable eval penalty, each found by a live run rather than a test: barwise-826 (constraint arity), barwise-830 (frequency bounds), and the population closed-world assumption in barwise-827.

The pattern is structural, not coincidental. enforceConformance exists to hand the parser something the validator will accept, so every purely STRUCTURAL rule in core/src/validation/rules/constraintConsistency.ts needs a mirror in conformance or it becomes an error the extraction cannot avoid. Nothing enforces that correspondence, so the gaps are found one eval run at a time.

Do this deliberately: enumerate every rule in constraintConsistency, classify each as structural (checkable on the extraction payload before model construction) or semantic (needs the built model), and confirm conformance mirrors every structural one. Removal is usually right for a malformed constraint -- it charges 0.02 as a correction rather than 0.1 as an error, which is the correct relative price.

Consider whether the correspondence can be made mechanical rather than remembered. A test that feeds deliberately-malformed constraints of every type through conformance and asserts the model validates clean would catch the next gap without a live run, though it needs a generator that knows what malformed means per type.
notes:
Audit complete. 19 rule ids across 20 diagnostic sites in constraintConsistency, classified structural/semantic in the spec.

One real gap found: constraint/ring-different-players (error, structural, unmirrored). A ring whose two roles are played by different object types survived conformance and the parser and landed in the model as an unavoidable validation error -- the same shape as barwise-826 and barwise-830. Fixed by conformance check 5c, which removes it and charges 0.02 as a correction rather than 0.1 as an error.

Most of the class turned out to be already closed, but by the PARSER rather than by conformance: seven invalid-role rules are unreachable because resolveRolesByPlayerName only returns ids drawn from the fact type it was handed, and the three cardinality rules are unreachable because the extraction vocabulary has no cardinality type. Recorded so a future auditor reading conformance alone does not add ten dead checks.

Two rules are correctly unmirrored: external-uniqueness-all-local and spanning-all-roles are modeling advisories, not defects.

The durable half is tests/ConstraintCorrespondence.test.ts: one malformed shape per type in the extraction vocabulary, asserting nothing surviving conformance produces a constraint/* ERROR (severity-scoped on purpose, so the two advisories are not forced into a wrong fix), plus a coverage test that fails if a new InferredConstraintType goes unswept. Verified by mutation: disabling the ring check fails 4 tests including the sweep entry.

title: Provenance called every run dirty because of untracked files
description:
resolveProvenance ran `git status --porcelain`, which lists untracked files as `??` entries. Any scratch note, editor swap file, or build output therefore marked a recorded eval run as having a modified tree, and `describeProvenance` printed `-dirty` on a checkout whose tracked source exactly matched the commit.

The compounding part is what makes it more than cosmetic: `history.jsonl` is neither tracked nor gitignored. So the FIRST run to record history created the untracked file that made every subsequent run report an unreproducible commit. The flag degraded to always-true the moment the feature it annotates started being used.

What dirty is for is deciding whether the recorded commit reproduces the run, so it has to mean the tracked source moved. Fixed with `--untracked-files=no`.

Untracked files are not entirely irrelevant -- an unversioned variant under --artifacts really would change what ran -- but promptHash already covers exactly that case by fingerprinting the prompt actually sent, rather than inferring it from the state of the working tree. Guessing from untracked files would be a worse instrument for the same question.

Reported by the user, who noticed dirty:true on a checkout where they had only untracked files and had changed nothing committed. Regression test builds a real git repo carrying the barwise marker and asserts clean, still clean with an untracked history.jsonl beside it, and dirty once a tracked file actually changes.

title: Eval scores could not explain themselves: unnamed warnings, discarded collapse payloads
description:
The first repeat=5 baseline produced a mean it could defend statistically and not explain mechanically.

university-enrollment: mean 0.540, sd 0.307, 4/5 surviving, quality 0.675, [corrections=1.6 warnings=6]. Two distinct problems averaging together -- six warnings costing 0.30 on EVERY run (systematic), and one run in five missing the CourseOffering entity entirely (variance, 76% of all suite noise). The collapse-floor split is what separated them; without it one number would have produced the wrong diagnosis.

Neither could be pursued further. scoreExtraction counted diagnostics by severity and discarded them, so the report could say six and not which six -- against seven completeness/* rules, none of which fire on the recorded answer keys, so the cost is addressable. And the payload of the collapsed run was scored and dropped, so there was no way to ask what it produced instead of CourseOffering.

Fixed per docs/specs/eval-diagnosis.spec.md: CaseScore.warningsByRule, a suite-level tally rendered under the report, CaseRun.payload kept ONLY for sub-floor and unscorable runs, and --save-payloads to write them.

History gains per-case penalty counts and the suite warning tally. Scoping note: HistoryEntry.tokens needed an argument because caching is score-neutral; warnings need none, being score-constitutive and ~80% of everything lost. A row carrying a mean without them cannot say whether a score moved because warnings fell or because a rubric check began passing. Per-rule detail stays suite-level -- seven rules across seven cases is forty-nine numbers answering a question nobody asks per case.

title: Extend the conformance/validator correspondence audit beyond constraintConsistency
description:
barwise-831 audited core/src/validation/rules/constraintConsistency.ts and found one real gap (ring player identity), plus a mechanical sweep that now guards that module: llm/tests/ConstraintCorrespondence.test.ts.

That audit was scoped to one rule module because the issue scoped it there. The same argument applies to every other rule module the extraction path can trip -- a purely structural rule with no conformance counterpart becomes a validation error the extraction cannot avoid, charged at 0.1 instead of the 0.02 a dropped malformed constraint costs.

Enumerate the other rule modules under core/src/validation/rules/, classify each rule structural or semantic the same way, and extend the sweep where a structural gap exists. Note that the constraintConsistency audit found most of its class already closed by the PARSER rather than by conformance -- check for that before adding a conformance check, or the result is dead code.

See docs/specs/constraint-conformance-audit.spec.md for the classification format and for why the sweep asserts on severity error rather than on diagnostics generally.
notes:
Audit complete, and the headline is the ratio: 51 error-severity sites across eight rule modules, ONE gap. Four of the five earlier finds in this class were real gaps, so a reader arriving from that run would expect a mess and would be wrong.

The gap: structural/subtype-cycle. Both edges of a two-node cycle resolve perfectly well, so the parser builds them and the model carries a cycle it is then rejected for. Conformance now drops the edge that CLOSES the cycle, keeping every relationship declared before it.

Everything else is unreachable, and by construction rather than luck: eleven of twelve structural rules are stopped because the parser resolves names against what it has already built and skips what it cannot; joinConstraintRules needs a joinPath nothing in llm/src ever builds; projectRules takes an OrmProject and extraction produces an OrmModel; population/cardinality needs ObjectType.cardinality, absent from the payload. Recorded so a future auditor does not add ~26 dead conformance checks.

Also worth knowing: the population/* modules are almost entirely WARNINGS, not errors -- a population contradicting a constraint is lint, not invalidity. That is why the population side is far less exposed than the constraint side, and it is not obvious from reading either module alone.

tests/StructuralCorrespondence.test.ts extends the mechanical sweep. It asserts the OUTCOME (no error reaches the model) rather than the mechanism, so a change moving responsibility between parser and conformance still passes while a parser admitting unresolved names fails. Verified by mutation: disabling the cycle check fails 5 tests.

title: Conformance check: every population instance must supply a value for every role
description:
Both prompt variants carry the line 'Every instance MUST supply a value for EVERY role of the fact type', and nothing in code enforces it -- cleanPopulations checks for empty instances, orphaned fact types, and populations duplicating a value constraint, but never that an individual instance is complete.

This is the one promotion candidate from barwise-813 that is squarely a deterministic check rather than a modelling judgement. The fact type's roles are known, the instance's role_values are known, and completeness is a set comparison. The other candidates cannot move: code can DETECT a missing uniqueness constraint (completeness/fact-type-without-uniqueness) but cannot decide whether it is many-to-one or many-to-many, and can detect a missing inverse reading (structural/binary-missing-inverse-reading) but cannot safely generate the inverse wording.

Follow the established shape: drop the incomplete instance (or the population, if that empties it) and record a correction, charging 0.02 rather than letting an invalid population reach the validator. Note the resolution nuance from barwise-831 -- role_values may be keyed by player name OR role name, so completeness must accept either spelling, the same way repairIdentifierPopulations already does when computing coverage.

Testable with no API calls, which is the point: it removes one line from what the paid measurement round in barwise-813 has to settle. See docs/specs/artifact-resolution-in-production.spec.md, 'Workstream 3, revisited'.
notes:
Done, and the investigation found a second, larger defect underneath the one filed.

As filed: population/incomplete-instance is an ERROR in the validator and conformance never checked it, so an instance short a role value cost 0.1. Conformance now drops the instance and charges 0.02 -- fourth instance of the barwise-826 class.

The larger defect: a self-referencing fact type could not have a valid population by ANY spelling. parsePopulations resolved role_values keys by player name only and took rolesForPlayer(...)[0], so on 'Employee mentors Employee' the player-name spelling {"Employee":"Alice"} can only carry one key (JSON forbids duplicates) and lost a role to incomplete-instance, while the role-name spelling failed to resolve and was dropped with a warning. Every ring and self-referencing fact type -- mentoring, prerequisites, org hierarchies, part-of -- was structurally incapable of carrying an example. No prompt text could have fixed that: the model was being asked for something the parser would not accept.

The fix aligns the two resolvers in the same package. parse/helpers.ts already did this correctly for CONSTRAINTS (role name first case-insensitively, then player name, each match consuming a role); parse/populations.ts now does the same. That is why the recorded project-staffing RING CONSTRAINT worked while a population of the same fact type could not.

Verified by mutation, not by being green: reverting the parser fails 2 tests, disabling the conformance check fails 4. All seven answer-key scores unchanged (the guard that mattered) and the full monorepo gate is green.

Consequence for barwise-813: the prompt bullet 'every instance MUST supply a value for every role' is now partly redundant with code, which is one more line the promotion round does not have to settle.

title: Record what the pipeline changed and what it could not fix
description:
Design proposal in docs/specs/pipeline-observability.spec.md. Sibling to barwise-815, which covers what a CALL cost; this covers what the pipeline DID to the payload.

Two concrete losses today.

1. Conformance corrections are structured at the source -- ConformanceCorrection {category, description, element} -- and TranscriptProcessor.ts:126 flattens them to warnings: string[] prose one line after enforceConformance returns them. The category is unrecoverable downstream, so no surface can count corrections by kind and nothing can be aggregated.

2. Validation diagnostics all carry a ruleId, and only the eval harness keeps any of it -- warningsByRule. Errors get a bare count in both the report and the history row. Errors cost 0.1, twice a warning, so the more expensive signal is the less diagnosable one.

The consequence was concrete: this session could not determine whether the ring-player fix (barwise-831) or the population fix (barwise-835) moved the recorded baselines, because the record counts errors without naming them. Not a measurement failure -- the runs were measured -- but the measurement was summed before it was stored.

Design constraint that decides the shape: corrections do NOT go on DraftModelResult. That type answers 'what model did this transcript produce and where did each part come from'; corrections answer 'what did a cleanup pass change'. observe/ is the component for the second, and it already exists. Note DraftModelResult already carries modelUsed/usage/latencyMs, which are call telemetry and belong in observe/ by the same argument -- deferred, not overlooked.

Extraction does not validate (ValidationEngine is constructed at 13 downstream sites), so these are two moments and get two records rather than one half-empty one.
notes:
Done, together with barwise-837 and workstream 2 of barwise-815 -- all three are the same seam and splitting them would have left the record half-written.

observe/extractionLog.ts is the sibling of callLog.ts: corrections recorded BY CATEGORY, parser warnings and skipped constraints as counts, plus what reached the model. processTranscript gained observer/now/correlationId and emits only when someone is listening.

Nothing was added to DraftModelResult, and a test asserts that directly rather than leaving the decision to review. The prose warnings are untouched -- surfaces render them to users, and a user who stopped being told their constraint was dropped would be worse off than before.

The no-content rule is tested over the SERIALISED record rather than field by field, because a field added later without thought is exactly how transcript text would leak.

Both import commands are wired, not one: batch.ts builds a client the same way, and wiring one of two is the divergence pattern this project keeps finding.

title: Errors are counted but never named: add errorsByRule alongside warningsByRule
description:
The smallest, highest-leverage piece of barwise-836, split out because it is independently shippable and blocks a decision that is waiting on it.

scoreExtraction returns warningsByRule (which rule warned, how many times) and validationErrors (a bare count). history.jsonl records penalties {corrections, errors, warnings} -- three counts. So a recorded run can say it had two validation errors and cannot say which rules produced them.

docs/specs/eval-diagnosis.spec.md closed exactly this gap for warnings on the argument that 'the count alone says a run lost 0.30 without saying to what'. The identical argument applies to errors and they cost twice as much.

Blocks the re-run decision: whether barwise-831 and barwise-835 moved the train/dev baselines is answerable from the record only if the record names the rule. Without this, the only way to find out is to spend money re-running, which is the wrong lever.

Must land in BOTH scoreExtraction and the history row -- adding it to one repeats the original defect one level up.
notes:
Done. errorsByRule landed in all four places -- CaseScore, the SuiteReport tally, the history row, and the CLI report -- because the spec's own risk note said both or neither: adding it to the scorer alone would have repeated the original defect one level up, which is exactly how the warning tally came to exist in one place and not the other.

The two tallies now share one helper in both the scorer and the runner. Two copies is how they came to differ in the first place.

The CLI prints errors above warnings, since errors cost twice as much and that line is what says whether a conformance fix actually landed.

Consequence for the re-run question: whether barwise-831 and barwise-835 moved the baselines is now answerable from any FUTURE run's record. It is still not answerable for the runs already recorded -- those rows carry penalties.errors as a bare count and nothing can retro-fit the identity. That is the cost of having shipped the asymmetry, and it is bounded now.

title: The validation-side observability record was specced and not built
description:
docs/specs/pipeline-observability.spec.md Scope asked observe/ for a record of what validation found, carrying each diagnostic's ruleId and severity. barwise-836 shipped the extraction-side record and named validation findings in PROMPTLAB (errorsByRule in the scorer, suite report, history row and CLI) -- which covers the eval harness and nothing else.

So the case the spec used to argue for keeping two moments apart is the case still unserved: ValidationEngine is constructed at 13 call sites, and a `barwise validate` on a hand-written model records nothing. The spec's own words -- 'exactly as worth recording as one that came from a transcript'.

What it needs: a ValidationRecord in observe/ (ruleId + severity, counts only -- diagnostic messages interpolate element names the transcript supplied, so the same no-content rule applies as for correction descriptions), plus a summarise helper, plus wiring at the surfaces that validate. Wire ALL of them or state which are deliberately out: wiring one of thirteen is the divergence pattern this project keeps finding, and barwise-836 wired both import commands rather than one for exactly that reason.

Filed against myself: the scope item was not implemented and the implementation notes did not flag it until a re-read caught it. A scope item silently unimplemented is the same defect as a capability matrix asserting parity that does not hold, which is what this spec was written about.
notes:
Done. observe/validationLog.ts carries errorsByRule and warningsByRule split by severity, with summariseValidation and emitValidationRecord following the same seam as the other two records (caller supplies clock and sink; a throwing sink is swallowed).

The info tier is deliberately neither counted nor tallied: it carries no weight in any score and recording it would grow every row for a tier nobody acts on. A diagnostic with no ruleId is recorded as (unattributed) rather than dropped -- dropping it would make the tally disagree with the count, which is the one failure this record exists to prevent.

Wired at `barwise validate` and nowhere else, which the issue asked me to state rather than assume. Of the 13 sites constructing a ValidationEngine, most are INTERNAL GATES rather than operations an operator asked for: the export formats validate before writing, learn's check runners validate as part of grading, and scoreExtraction already records the same tallies through the eval harness. Logging those would turn one `barwise export` into several validation events -- noise, not observability. MCP is the one worth revisiting when a sink exists on that surface.

title: orphaned_reference_mode charges 0.02 for a condition core rates 'info', and mirrors no validator rule
description:
Surfaced by correctionsByCategory the moment it existed. Scoring the seven recorded answer keys gives 14 conformance corrections and ALL FOURTEEN are one category: orphaned_reference_mode. Those payloads carry zero validation errors and zero warnings, so at 0.02 each this single rule is the entire gap between them and 1.0 (their scores run 0.94-0.98).

Two things make it worth a decision rather than a shrug.

1. It is DETECT-ONLY. checkOrphanedReferenceModes records a correction saying an entity has a reference_mode with no identifier fact type, and changes nothing. Every other category removes or repairs something; this one is charged the same 0.02 for noticing. 'Correction' is arguably the wrong word for it, and the weight is arguably the wrong price.

2. It is a FLOOR under every case, so it is baked into every recorded baseline and into the barwise-813 promotion decision without anyone having chosen it.

The question is which of three: (a) the detection is right and the charge is right -- an entity with a reference mode and no identifier fact type really is an incomplete extraction, and the prompt should be taught to emit the identifier fact type; (b) the detection is right but detect-only findings should not be charged as corrections, in which case it wants its own tier; (c) the detection is too eager -- a reference mode without an identifier fact type may be perfectly acceptable in a draft -- and it should not fire at all.

Do NOT change the weight before deciding which. Every recorded history row prices this rule at 0.02, so a reweight silently reinterprets the whole record -- the failure mode barwise-836 exists to stop. (a) needs no weight change at all and is testable against the answer keys for free.
notes:
INVESTIGATED 2026-08-23. The evidence points to option (c) -- the detection is too eager -- and more sharply than the issue anticipated. Four findings, each checked against the source:

1. NO VALIDATOR COUNTERPART. Every other conformance check exists to prevent a specific validator error; that is the whole justification of the module. Nothing in core/src/validation/rules/ mentions referenceMode at all. This check mirrors nothing -- it invents a rule.

2. CORE RATES THE NEAREST THING 'info', WHICH COSTS ZERO. completeness/missing-preferred-identifier is severity info and its message says the relational mapper will use a heuristic. So core's own position is that an entity without an explicit identifier is FINE. Conformance charges 0.02 for it -- more than core charges for the closest real diagnostic.

3. THE PARSER MANUFACTURES A REFERENCE MODE FOR EVERY ENTITY. parse/objectTypes.ts does `ext.reference_mode ?? camelCase(name) + '_id'`, because ObjectType THROWS if an entity has none. A reference mode is mandatory, not optional metadata, so 'has a reference mode' is not evidence of anything.

4. IT FLAGS WHAT THE NOTATION IS FOR. In ORM 2, Patient (medical_record_number) IS the shorthand for the identifier fact type. Every one of the 14 answer-key hits is an ordinary reference mode -- sku, employee_id, room_number -- on an entity modelled exactly as ORM intends. The check asks the extraction to spell out the thing the notation abbreviates.

Plus the evidence that started this: it fired 0 times across 15 live dev runs and 14 times across 7 hand-curated answer keys. It is not measuring extraction quality.

RECOMMENDATION: remove the check (option c). Consequence worth seeing before agreeing -- all 14 answer-key corrections are this rule, so removing it takes every recorded answer key from 0.94-0.98 to exactly 1.000. That is arguably the point: the reference payloads should score 1.0, and they do not solely because of a check that mirrors nothing.

NOT DONE OVERNIGHT, DELIBERATELY. Any change here -- removing it, or keeping the detection while not charging it -- moves the answer-key pins in scoreExtraction.test.ts and makes every recorded history row incomparable, including the dev baseline measured hours earlier. That is the same 'do not land it between two runs being compared' hazard flagged on barwise-840, and this one is 14 corrections rather than 1 error. It needs a yes, not an inference from a sleeping reviewer, and it is a one-word decision now that the evidence is in.

CLOSED 2026-08-23: option (c), removal, approved by the user and implemented. docs/specs/reference-mode-charge-removal.spec.md.

checkOrphanedReferenceModes, its call site and identifierFactTypeEntities (which nothing else read) are gone. All seven recorded answer keys now score exactly 1.000, up from 0.94-0.98.

SUITE VERSION BUMPED 1.2.0 -> 1.3.0. It changes no case, no weight and no floor; it marks a change outside the manifest with the same consequence, since every payload scored under 1.2.0 carried a charge that no longer exists. The version is the field a reader uses to decide whether two history rows can be compared, and after this they cannot.

WORTH CARRYING FORWARD. Two tests were leaning on an answer key being imperfect: the weights-and-floor test needed three corrections to exist, and the penalties-reach-the-history-row test read the one correction every key happened to carry. Both now manufacture their own penalty. That dependency is exactly how this check became load-bearing without anyone choosing it -- the issue's own framing ('a floor under every case, baked into every recorded baseline') turned out to hold inside the test suite too.

Also: two collapse-floor tests used 0.999 as 'above every achievable score'. With clean answer keys that no longer holds, so both now use 1.001. A test that silently stops testing what it names is the barwise-840 failure mode.

A regression test asserts the charge does NOT happen, carrying all four findings inline so the next reader does not re-derive the question and re-add the check.

Full gate green: 1403 core, 418 llm, 154 promptlab, 219 cli, 179 mcp, 69 vscode.

title: Conformance counts role hints; the parser counts resolved roles, so duplicate hints bypass the arity check
description:
Found by the first diagnostic round with errorsByRule (2026-08-23 dev sweep, haiku-4-5, default artifact). One validation error in fifteen runs, and it is a rule conformance is supposed to make impossible: constraint/disjunctive-mandatory-too-few-roles on incident-response.

Reproduced deterministically. isValidArity checks ic.roles.length -- the number of role HINTS the model emitted. resolveRolesByPlayerName consumes each role it matches, so two hints naming the same player resolve to ONE role id. Conformance sees 2 and passes it; the parser builds a disjunctive_mandatory with a single roleId; the validator rejects it. 0.1 the extraction could not avoid.

  roles: ['Incident', 'Incident']  ->  conformance: length 2, ok
                                    ->  parser: 1 resolved role
                                    ->  validator: must reference at least 2 roles

Sixth instance of the barwise-826 class, and the first that is not a MISSING check but a check measuring the wrong quantity. My barwise-831 sweep missed it because every probe used distinct resolvable names -- the sweep tested the check's existence, not its arithmetic.

Fix: resolve the hints in conformance the way the parser does (role name first case-insensitively, then player name, each match consuming a role -- the discipline barwise-835 already aligned parse/populations.ts to) and apply the arity rule to the RESOLVED count. Applies to every arity branch, not just disjunctive_mandatory: ring (exactly 2), mandatory/frequency/value_constraint (exactly 1), exclusion and exclusive_or (at least 2).

Extend StructuralCorrespondence/ConstraintCorrespondence with duplicate-hint variants; the existing sweeps pass today and would still pass after a wrong fix.

Cost is small -- 1 error in 15 runs, 1.9% of the dev penalty -- so this is a correctness fix, not a score fix. Note it WILL move recorded baselines slightly, so land it before the next measurement round rather than between two runs being compared.
notes:
Fixed. The investigation found THREE bypass paths, not the one the issue described -- all producing the same unavoidable error, all invisible to the existing sweep:

  A  ['Incident','Incident']          one role named twice (consuming resolution)
  B  ['Incident','Customer']          check 4's name set is GLOBAL, not per fact type, so a
                                      real object type that plays no role here passes it
  C  ['originates from','Incident']   a role name and a player name selecting one role

The arity check now measures the RESOLVED count, and deliberately only for disjunctive_mandatory, exclusion and exclusive_or. That scope is exact, not approximate: every other type the parser skips outright when the resolved count is wrong, and a skipped constraint never reaches the validator -- so checking them here would charge 0.02 for constraints already dropped for free, which is a score change dressed as a correctness fix and would land on every recorded baseline at once. The two uniqueness types do build on a short resolution, but uniqueness over one role is valid ORM.

One resolver (resolveRoleIndices) now serves the arity check, the ring-player check and population completeness. Three copies of a consuming name match is precisely how this divergence grew in the first place.

Verified by mutation: disabling the check fails 9 tests, 3 of them sweep entries. Ten hand-checked probes confirm the three paths close, valid constraints are untouched, uniqueness over one role still builds, and ring gains no new charge. All seven answer-key scores unchanged; full gate green (419 llm, 154 promptlab, 211 cli).

Worth carrying: the sweep passed throughout because every probe used distinct resolvable names. It asserted the check EXISTED and never that its arithmetic was right -- the same failure mode one level in from the one barwise-831 was written about.

title: prompt eval has never run without an API key, so every line it prints is unverified
description:
barwise prompt eval is the one command in the repo that has never been held to the determinism preference: every line it prints has only ever executed with an API key in the environment. promptlab/tests/runSuite.test.ts covers the runner with a fixture client, but nothing covers what the CLI does around it -- artifact resolution and its version line, the incomplete-run warning and exitCode 1, the truncation warning, --save-payloads, the history append and its provenance, and createLlmClient from flags with the budget it derives. Each of those is a line an operator reads while a sweep is running, or a file they rely on afterwards, and a wrong one costs the round that discovered it.

Instrument: a loopback ollama server, not an injected mock client. The CLI builds its own client from its own flags, and that construction is part of what is untested -- injecting past it would test a path no operator takes while leaving the real one uncovered, and would put a production seam in place solely for a test. The ollama provider already takes --base-url, speaks a documented NDJSON protocol over fetch, and returns the payload as bare content, which is exactly the shape the recorded fixtures hold. So nothing in barwise is stubbed; the fake is the server.

Seven train cases run in about half a second, against roughly twenty minutes and real money for the same sweep against Anthropic.

See docs/specs/offline-eval-rehearsal.spec.md.
notes:
Implemented 2026-08-23. Eight tests in cli/tests/commands/promptEvalOffline.test.ts over a fake server in cli/tests/workspace/fakeOllama.ts. No production code changed -- if the spec had required any, the design would have been wrong.

Mutation-checked: seven deliberate breakages, each caught by exactly one test. One-for-one is the result worth recording; a mutation tripping four tests says they overlap and one tripping none says the assertion was decorative.

The sharpest of the seven: resolve the variant and then never pass it to runSuite. The 'Using artifact version' line stays intact and the default prompt goes on the wire -- a comparative round that reports the variant it never ran. Only reading the system prompt back off the wire catches it, which is why that assertion is there rather than a check on stderr.

Two hazards found by building it, both recorded in the spec because the symptom points nowhere near the cause:
1. Node's fetch pools connections, so server.close() waits on a socket that is never coming back and the test process hangs after the assertions pass. The first probe hung four minutes. Teardown must call closeAllConnections().
2. historyPathFor is dirname(manifest)/history.jsonl, so a test running the packaged suite would append to the repository's own recorded history. Every test copies evals/ to a temp dir first. A score record a test can write to is not a record.

Incidental confirmation of barwise-839: the rehearsal reproduces the answer-key means exactly (0.98 0.96 0.96 0.94 0.98 0.96 0.94) and reports 'fixed: orphaned_reference_mode x14' as the entire penalty.

title: prompt eval resolves the artifact from flags, not from the client, so omitting --provider silently runs the default prompt
description:
Confirmed deterministically against the built resolver (2026-08-23):

  --provider anthropic --model claude-haiku-4-5   -> haiku45-2
  --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-5    -> sonnet5-3
  (no --provider)     --model claude-haiku-4-5    -> DEFAULT ARTIFACT

prompt eval passes opts.provider and opts.model -- the FLAGS -- into resolveArtifact. When --provider is omitted the CLI still builds a working client, because createLlmClient auto-detects the provider from env vars, but resolveArtifact is handed provider: undefined and no variant can match its 'provider: anthropic' clause. The run then uses the default prompt while the operator believes it used the variant they passed --artifacts for.

The client already knows the answer. LlmClient declares provider and model precisely so a variant can be resolved before the call -- that is the documented reason the fields exist (packages/llm/CLAUDE.md, 'A client declares its own identity'), and processTranscript resolves from the client. The eval command resolves from the flags instead, so the two disagree about what provider is in play. Same shape as the rest of this session's findings: a value the system had already computed, discarded at a boundary in favour of a weaker one.

Mitigating: the command does print 'Using the default prompt artifact.' and that line is truthful. It is easy to miss at the head of a sweep that then runs for twenty minutes.

NOT a silent failure to fix casually. Resolving from the client would also change a run that passes neither --provider nor --model: today that gets the default artifact, and afterwards it would get whichever variant matches the anthropic default model. That is a real behaviour change to a plausible command line, so it wants a decision rather than a patch, and it must not land between two runs being compared.

Found by barwise-841's mutation check, which asks exactly this question: does the command send the variant it says it resolved? The mutation was hypothetical; this is the same failure reachable through ordinary flag usage.
notes:
Fixed 2026-08-25 as part of barwise-850. Resolution moved to AFTER the client is built and now keys on client.provider / client.model rather than opts.provider / opts.model. createLlmClient auto-detects the provider and every provider resolves its own default model (AnthropicLlmClient.model is `readonly model: string`, defaulted), so a client built with neither flag knows both -- which is the documented reason LlmClient carries them.

Grounding corrected the issue's scope: the bug was worse than filed. Omitting --provider was not the only way to get the default -- prompt eval never consulted builtinArtifacts under ANY flags, because resolution sat behind `if (opts.artifacts)`. See barwise-850.

Regression test: promptEvalOffline 'resolves the variant from the client's model, not from the --model flag'. Ollama defaults to llama3.1, which no flag mentions, so only a client-side resolution finds a variant matching modelPrefix llama3. Mutation-checked.

title: Build the DSPy optimizer lane (harness workstream 3), never grounded since 2026-08-08
description:
Workstream 3 of docs/specs/prompt-optimization-harness.spec.md, carried as 'provisional: not yet grounded' since 2026-08-08 and never built. Requested directly.

The lane: a Python project under barwise/optimizer/, uv-managed, outside the npm workspace, never imported, never in CI, never on the runtime path. It crosses to TypeScript only through two subprocess calls -- barwise prompt schema and barwise prompt score -- which already exist as ordinary commands. No shared library, no FFI, no second copy of the schema or the scorer.

Grounding the harness spec asked for, now measured. (1) dspy 3.3.1 installs with BootstrapFewShot, MIPROv2, GEPA, COPRO. (2) DSPy renders its own field protocol around the instructions, which production never emits -- so the compiled program's score is a SEARCH SIGNAL and the accepted number always comes from a real barwise prompt eval. (3) Demos do not fit naively: the system prompt is ~4,540 tokens and demo payloads run 1,103-3,851 (mean 1,984), so BootstrapFewShot's 4-16 default is a 3x-8x prompt paid on every call of every candidate. The exporter budgets and truncates; the compile step caps demos at 2.

See docs/specs/dspy-optimizer.spec.md.
notes:
Implemented 2026-08-23. 55 tests, about a minute, no API key and no network.

THE RESOLUTION PROBLEM IS BUILT IN RATHER THAN ARGUED ABOUT. At repeat=5 the suite's resolvable difference is ~0.086, and DSPy is the technique most sensitive to that. So: --max-calls and --samples-per-candidate are REQUIRED (no library default for anything that costs money), samples below 2 is refused because the run could not then report a spread, and every run writes a delta report that leads with whether the margin cleared the noise band and labels one inside it as not evidence. The metric also records errorsByRule / warningsByRule / correctionsByCategory per evaluation, so the report says WHICH NAMED RULE MOVED -- a count from the same calls, legible where a 0.03 shift in a mean is not.

FOUR BUGS FOUND WHILE BUILDING, none visible from reading the code:

1. MIPROv2 reads dspy.settings.lm in its constructor and raises without one; BootstrapFewShot constructs happily and fails much later. The same ordering mistake read as 'mipro is broken'. build_optimizer now requires an LM uniformly.
2. GEPA requires a separate reflection_lm. --proposer-model was already recorded in provenance but never wired to the optimizer that needs it -- a value computed and dropped at a boundary, the same class as everything else this week. Now wired, and gepa without one is refused at config time so it costs a flag rather than a run.
3. The exported instructions carried the 11.5 KB schema (candidate: 20 KB), duplicating in every request what production sends as the tool's input_schema, and handing MIPROv2 a schema to paraphrase. Schema moved to the output field description.
4. THE CANDIDATE HAD NO match BLOCK. resolveArtifact filters to artifacts declaring one, so it loaded without complaint and was silently skipped -- the operator would read 'Using the default prompt artifact.' while believing they had gated the candidate they paid to compile. Same failure class as barwise-842 one layer out. match is now required and derived from the target model.

3 and 4 were found by SMOKE-RUNNING run() offline, and 4 specifically by round-tripping the export through the real prompt eval --artifacts loader rather than asserting on the exporter's own YAML, which would only have proved the package agrees with itself. Both are now tests.

Mutation-checked: eight deliberate breakages, each caught; the last two only by the smoke test and the loader round trip.

NOT DONE, deliberately: running a real compilation. The lane is built; spending money on it is a separate human act, and the run report exists so that when someone does, the result says what it can support.
