TWO REAL COMPILATIONS RUN (2026-08-24), bootstrap on claude-haiku-4-5, 32 calls each.

RUN 1, --seed-from minimal. Both arms floored at 0 (penalties ~0.98 and ~1.02/run against a rubric fraction of at most 1.0). Uninterpretable as a comparison, but it produced two design corrections (the saturation guard and --seed-from itself) and one real result: demos fixed format adherence, unparseable 5 -> 0 across 15 evaluations. That is barwise-812's question answered on real content.

RUN 2, --seed-from default (haiku45-2). Clean: floored 0, unparseable 0.
  baseline  mean 0.870   10 corrections, 35 warnings -> 0.130/run penalty
  candidate mean 0.840   20 corrections, 40 warnings -> 0.160/run penalty
  margin -0.030 against a resolvable difference of 0.0999 -- INSIDE the noise band.

Both arms reconcile to the digit, which means rubricPassed == rubricTotal on every evaluation: haiku passes the whole rubric on all three held-out cases every time, and the entire gap from 1.0 is penalty rather than missing content.

VERDICT: do not adopt. The candidate is nominally worse and the difference does not resolve. The demos drove arity_mismatch 5 -> 20 (a count, not a mean, so a real pattern) while fixing duplicate_constraint 5 -> 0. Bootstrap's demos are the model's own outputs, so it propagates whatever the traces got wrong -- the same feedback loop as run 1, milder.

THE REMAINING TARGET IS ONE RULE. completeness/fact-type-without-constraints at 30 occurrences = 0.100/run = 77% of the entire remaining penalty. That is an instruction problem, so it wants mipro rather than bootstrap; bootstrap cannot touch instructions at all.

INCIDENTAL, FOR BARWISE-813. Against the earlier dev diagnostic on the DEFAULT artifact (same 3 cases, same 5 samples): fact-type-without-uniqueness 18 -> 0, fact-type-without-constraints 50 -> 30. Warning counts are unaffected by the 839 correction removal, so they compare across the suite bump. Direct evidence that haiku45-2 beats the default on exactly the rules its bullets target. CAVEAT: the earlier numbers came through the production path and these through DSPy's adapter, which renders differently -- suggestive, not clean. A `prompt eval --artifacts packages/llm/prompts --provider anthropic --model claude-haiku-4-5 --split dev --repeat 5` would settle it through the real renderer for ~15 calls and append a comparable history row.

title: Eval penalties are counted, not rated, so a bigger model is charged more for the same defect rate
description:
scoreExtraction computes rubricPassed/rubricTotal (bounded to [0,1]) minus sum(weight * occurrences) (unbounded, growing with model size). The reward side is normalised and the penalty side is not, so the same defect RATE costs a large model several times what it costs a small one.

Measured from the recorded compilations: on the dev split, structural/binary-missing-inverse-reading occurred at a mean of 10.67 per scored run; at validationWarning 0.05 that one rule costs 0.53. The train reference models hold a median of 3 fact types in total, so the same rule at a 100% defect rate costs a median train case 0.15. Same rate, 3.5x the charge, decided entirely by transcript length.

Past 1.0 the clamp in scoreExtraction takes over and the damage compounds: floored arms all report 0.000 however different they were, and the identical values collapse the sample SD, shrinking resolvableDifference so a meaningless margin can clear a threshold the flooring itself manufactured. Three of the four recorded compilation arms floored.

Fix: penalty(rule) = weight * occurrences / max(elementCount, 1), with elementCount = objectTypes + factTypes recorded on CaseScore. The weight then means the cost of a model in which every element carries that defect. Weights must be re-fitted in the same change and the suite bumps to 2.0.0.

The answer-key invariant survives untouched (zero occurrences over any denominator is zero, so all seven keys still score 1.000) -- which means it CANNOT detect a wrong denominator. Mutation-check by inverting it, and pin at least one non-perfect score.

Workstream 1 of the spec.

DECIDED 2026-08-24: weights are validationWarning 0.4, validationError 0.8, conformanceCorrection 0.2, read as 'a model in which every element carries a warning loses 0.4'. Checked against the recorded dev run first: at an estimated 24 elements the two dominant rules cost about 0.27 together under these weights against 0.81 under today's, close to the 3x distortion being removed. ambiguityExcess stays at 0.02 and stays UNRATED -- it is already charged against a per-case authored budget, so rating it would divide twice.

One denominator for every rule, not per-rule denominators. The approximation was measured: across the seven reference models fact types are 33-50% of total elements and the dominant rules all fire on fact types, so the denominator is wrong by a near-constant factor, which a weight absorbs. Per-rule denominators would make every new validator rule a promptlab change. Retrofitting them later costs a second re-baselining and that was accepted knowingly.

title: The three realism eval cases have no reference model, so the dev split carries zero forbids_population checks
description:
The train and dev splits do not grade the same thing. Across the ten cases:

  forbids_population   train 14 total   dev 0
  requires_ambiguity   train 0          dev 2
  requires_element     train 2-3/case   dev 4-5/case
  reference model      train all 7      dev none

forbids_population is the only check that tests whether a constraint actually forbids what it should -- the evaluator derives a counterexample population from the reference and requires the candidate to reject it. It exists in train and nowhere else. So train grades constraint semantics and dev grades element recall, and a change improving one is under no obligation to improve the other.

This is why the mipro run's reading was wrong: its own metric rose 50.89 -> 52.97 while every held-out figure fell, and that was recorded as the split catching overfitting. The split may have caught that; it cannot be used as evidence of it, because the two numbers never measured one quantity.

The cause is mechanical rather than an oversight: references are generated by running a recorded payload through parseExtractionFromJson, no payload has ever been recorded for these three (vendor-onboarding.eval.yaml:7-9 says so), loadSuite refuses a forbids_population check without a reference, and the rubrics were authored around the gap.

Fix: record a payload for vendor-onboarding, subscription-billing and incident-response; generate their references; add forbids_population where the transcript settles a constraint, and a requires_ambiguity check to incident-response, which has none despite being a realism case.

Workstream 2 of the spec. Separable from the re-split and worth landing first -- it is the cheapest step that makes the two halves comparable at all.
close_reason: Closed at suite 2.5.0 from the 2026-08-27 haiku45-2 sweep's saved payloads. All three dev cases now carry generated references (best payload per case: vendor-onboarding-run3 at 1.000, subscription-billing-run4 at 0.994, incident-response-run2 at 0.960), fifteen forbids_population checks where the transcripts settle constraints, incident-response's requires_ambiguity plus ambiguityBudget 10, and the suite's first irreflexive ring check with a genuine answer key. Both halves now grade constraint semantics. Answer keys pinned in scoreExtraction.test.ts (two pin below 1.000 over recorded-payload conformance defects, deliberately).

title: Stratify the eval splits so train and dev are two samples of one population, then re-baseline at 2.0.0
description:
Even with rubric parity (barwise-845) the splits stay confounded on transcript shape: train is 154-243 words of single-expert interview, dev is 2,163-2,967 words of multi-party disagreement. Every property that made the three realism cases worth adding is also a property that distinguishes dev from train, because eval-transcript-realism workstream 2 added them and made them the entire dev split in one change.

Fix: author new realistic transcripts so each split carries cases at each size class, then reassign splits so neither half is identifiable from its rubric or its transcript length. Then re-baseline both splits at repeat >= 5 for the default artifact and both committed variants, write the first committed rows of evals/history.jsonl, and re-fit collapseFloor against that distribution rather than the seven-case evidence it was fitted to.

TIMING: evals/history.jsonl does not exist in the repository. historyPathFor resolves it beside the manifest, provenance.ts:57 records that it is untracked, and no run has ever written one here. The continuity that eval-metric-readiness cited as the reason to keep the seven in train lives only in operators' local files, so the re-split is nearly free today and gets monotonically more expensive the moment the first committed rows land. Re-check that before starting -- it is the anchor most likely to have gone stale.

Workstreams 3 and 4 of the spec. Blocked on barwise-844: the number of new cases needed depends on dispersion measured after the penalties are rated.

DECIDED 2026-08-24: three new long transcripts, giving 7 short and 6 long -- train 4 short + 3 long, dev 3 short + 3 long. One new long case is the minimum that removes the confound; the extra two buy a six-case dev half over a four-case one. If the dev error bar is still wide at six cases, raise repeat rather than authoring a seventh: samples cost API calls and cases cost authored domains.

Also decided: 'no client-derived material in evals/' is now a stated rule in packages/promptlab/CLAUDE.md, written when the decision was made rather than deferred to this workstream.
notes: Workstream 3's authoring plan is now specced: docs/specs/eval-difficulty-calibration.spec.md (device taxonomy D1-D5, five candidate domains, recommended trio BOM/clinical-trial/curriculum, both-splits-per-device rule). The 2026-08-27 sweep grounded the case count: dev sd 0.044 with one case carrying ~90% of it says three new cases stand. Open decisions in the spec: domain trio, split placement of the D4 carrier (dev has no reification case), where the parked subset rule rides.

title: reviewModel never resolves a prompt artifact, so the review surface cannot be versioned, hashed or evaluated
acceptance_criteria: reviewModel resolves a surface: "review" artifact from builtinArtifacts using the client's declared provider and model, with an optional artifact override on ReviewOptions; a golden test pins the default rendered prompt byte-for-byte against the pre-wiring literal; parseReviewResponse rejects a suggestion whose category or severity falls outside its enum; the three call sites (CLI, MCP, VS Code) are unchanged.
description:
PromptSurface is declared as "extraction" | "review", loadArtifact accepts both, and resolveArtifact is generic over the pair -- but every artifact in packages/llm/prompts/ declares surface: extraction and reviewModel never calls the resolver. Its prompt is a string literal returned by buildReviewSystemPrompt(). The type says two surfaces are supported; one is.

Same shape as barwise-811, and the more expensive instance: review is the one LLM capability reachable from all three surfaces (CLI, MCP and VS Code all call reviewModel), so everything the extraction lane learned about prompt quality is unavailable to the surface with the widest reach.

The call sites need no change. LlmClient carries provider and model precisely so a variant can be chosen before the call, and TranscriptProcessor.ts:116 already resolves from the client rather than from its caller; review can do the same in the same place.

Also in scope, because the metric depends on it: parseReviewResponse casts obj.suggestions to ReviewSuggestion[] without validating category or severity against their enums. A model answering category: "style" produces a typed lie today and would silently match no planted defect once scoring exists.

Acceptance criterion: a golden test asserting the default rendered prompt is byte-identical to the current literal.

Workstream 1 of the spec.
close_reason: Workstream 1 of docs/specs/review-surface-evals.spec.md. reviewModel now resolves a review artifact from builtinArtifacts using the client's own provider and model, falling back to defaultReviewArtifact (the historical literal); ReviewOptions gains an optional artifact, and an artifact of the wrong surface is rejected before the LLM call. parseReviewResponse validates each suggestion against the declared category and severity enums (and the required string fields) and drops the malformed ones rather than casting the array. A golden fixture pins the default prompt's 2,609 bytes; every new assertion was mutation-checked. The three call sites needed no change, as the spec's Inventory promised. No review artifact was added, so the resolution is a no-op today. Full monorepo build, test and lint green.

title: Add ReviewEvalCase and scoreReview: seeded-defect recall with a clean control for precision
description:
The review surface has no metric. Grading advice looks like it needs a judge, which the harness refuses on principle. It dissolves once the question changes from 'was this good advice' to 'did it find the thing that is wrong': plant a known defect in a fixture model and either a suggestion names that element in that category or none does. ReviewSuggestion already carries element and category, so the payload has both fields a match needs.

Recall alone is winnable by volume. The extraction lane hit exactly this with requires_ambiguity and answered with ambiguityBudget; the same answer works here, and the second half is cheaper still -- run the reviewer on the UNMUTATED model, where every suggestion is a false positive by construction and no authoring is needed at all.

That makes the clean control a case with an empty defect list rather than a special mode: one case shape, no branch, graded by the same fold.

  score = found / max(defects, 1)
          - suggestionExcess * max(0, suggestions - defects - budget)

A case with no defects scores on the excess term alone. Matching is case-insensitive containment on element plus exact category; a suggestion with no element matches nothing.

Review cases get their own manifest and version -- one version: cannot describe two metrics, and the version is the field a reader uses to decide whether two history rows compare.

Workstream 2 of the spec. Independent of barwise-847: the scorer grades a payload and does not care how the prompt was built.

DECIDED 2026-08-24: excess is CHARGED as one scalar, matching ambiguityExcess -- reporting recall and suggestion count as a pair hands every consumer the collapse decision, the shape the sibling spec rejects for the extraction score.

Matching rule: a defect is found when some suggestion IN ITS CATEGORY names the element case-insensitively, in `element` or -- when that field is absent -- in `description`. A suggestion naming the element nowhere matches nothing. Strict field-only matching would score a model that names the element in prose as having missed the defect, which measures formatting; category-only matching would let a vague summary claim every find.

Suite selection: the manifest declares `surface: review` and `barwise prompt eval` reads it. No --suite flag and no second subcommand -- a flag and a manifest can disagree about what a suite is, and a manifest alone cannot. A manifest with no declared surface means extraction, which is what every existing manifest means today.

title: Author the review eval seed corpus, baseline it, and decide whether the review prompt is worth optimizing
description:
Paired fixtures: a clean base model per domain and a defective twin per review category, plus a control case per pair. The pairing is the design -- twins differ only by the planted defects, so a difference between the two cases cannot be attributed to size, domain or serialization.

Fixtures are authored rather than generated. Mechanical mutation was considered and set aside: four of the five categories mechanise cleanly and normalization does not (a missing subtype or a redundant fact type is a judgment about the domain, not an edit), so a new subsystem would buy four-fifths of the corpus. @barwise/core has no mutation machinery today; counterexample/ and diff/ are the closest and neither seeds defects.

Open before authoring: how many planted defects a case can carry before they interfere. A model with a stripped definition and a dropped constraint on the same element may draw one suggestion naming both, and whether that is one find or two is a question the fixtures answer rather than the design. Until it is answered, plant at most one defect per element.

Then baseline each supported provider/model pair at repeat >= 5 and READ THE RESULT BEFORE WRITING ANY OPTIMIZER PROGRAM. If the shipped literal already finds nearly every planted defect, this lane is a regression detector and not an optimization target, and saying so is a result. A first baseline near 100% recall is more likely a sign the corpus is too easy.

Workstreams 3 and 4 of the spec.

DECIDED 2026-08-24: two domains, each with one clean base model, five defective twins (one per review category, each the base with a single edit) and one control case scoring the clean base with an empty defect list. Twelve cases in all. The authoring cost is dominated by the shared base, so this costs barely more than one defective model carrying all five categories and yields recall PER CATEGORY -- weak normalization recall and weak definition recall call for different prompt changes. Four categories are a mechanical edit; normalization needs a modelling judgment.

Also decided: NO prompt caching on the review call. Measured rather than deferred -- the review system prompt is 2,609 characters, about 650 tokens, against Haiku 4.5's 4,096-token minimum cacheable prefix, so a breakpoint is inert on the model the suite runs against. Revisit only if the prompt grows past 4,096.

title: prompt eval never consulted builtinArtifacts, so the shipped variants have never been evaluated
description:
Artifact resolution in `prompt eval` sat behind `if (opts.artifacts)` (prompt.ts:124). Without a directory the command never looked at `builtinArtifacts` at all -- it passed `artifact: undefined` to runSuite, which renders the default directly (runSuite.ts:352). `--provider` and `--model` reached the client but never the artifact query.

So the same two flags gave two answers from one tool:

  prompt artifact --provider anthropic --model claude-haiku-4-5  -> haiku45-2
  prompt eval     --provider anthropic --model claude-haiku-4-5  -> 1.0.0 (default)

The shipped variants are compiled into builtins.generated.ts, so haiku45-2 and sonnet5-3 -- the prompts production actually sends -- had never once been measured by the command built to measure them. Every recorded row measured the default while naming a provider and a model.

No error, ever: resolution returning undefined is indistinguishable from an operator deliberately choosing the default, and the stderr line said only 'Using the default prompt artifact.'

FIXED alongside barwise-851 and barwise-842: one `artifactCandidates` module builds the set for both commands, and the fallback message now names the provider/model that matched nothing.
close_reason: Fixed by artifactCandidates (cli/src/workspace/promptArtifacts.ts): prompt eval now resolves over builtinArtifacts plus any --artifacts dir, so the shipped variants are measurable. Per docs/specs/artifact-resolution-parity.spec.md

title: prompt artifact double-loads the builtins when --artifacts points at the directory they are generated from
description:
`prompt artifact` built `[...builtinArtifacts, ...loadArtifactsFromDir(dir)]`. Point --artifacts at packages/llm/prompts/ -- the very files builtins.generated.ts is generated FROM -- and the resolver sees haiku45-2 twice and refuses:

  Error: Ambiguous prompt artifacts ... version haiku45-2 (provider=anthropic, modelPrefix=claude-haiku); version haiku45-2 (provider=anthropic, modelPrefix=claude-haiku)

A comment claimed order settled it -- 'built-ins first, then the directory, so a local variant can win against a shipped one of equal specificity rather than colliding with it'. resolveArtifact compares specificity and knows nothing of order, so the claim was never true.

This is the same defect as barwise-850 seen from the other side: the two commands built their candidate set differently, one ignoring the builtins and one double-counting them.

FIXED: `artifactCandidates` de-duplicates by version with the directory winning. A directory entry sharing a builtin's version IS that builtin, edited. Two variants at equal specificity under DIFFERENT versions stay ambiguous and still throw.
close_reason: Fixed by artifactCandidates: directory entries de-duplicate builtins by version (a local file sharing a builtin version IS that builtin, edited), so pointing --artifacts at packages/llm/prompts/ no longer refuses as ambiguous

title: university-enrollment is bimodal, and it manufactures 88% of the suite's resolvable difference
description:
First 2.0.0 baseline, train split, haiku 4.5, repeat=5, default artifact:

  university-enrollment  0.080  0.961  0.154  0.070  0.906   sd=0.457

Two clusters, not a spread. The rubric output names the mechanism: the model either invents `CourseOffering` or it does not, and when it does not, three requires_element and two forbids_population checks fail together as one correlated block -- five of six checks flipping on a single modelling decision.

The run reports '88% of that noise is university-enrollment alone'. Suite resolvable difference is 0.087. Removing that variance takes SD to about 0.35 of current and resolvable to roughly 0.030 -- a 3x gain in discriminating power from one case.

That matters because docs/specs/dspy-optimizer.spec.md concluded the MEASUREMENT was the binding constraint: resolvable ~0.10 against 0.13 of headroom on the shipped prompt. At 0.03 the optimizer has real room.

Not yet diagnosed: whether the transcript underdetermines CourseOffering (an authoring bug, fix the transcript) or whether it is genuinely hard and the model is genuinely inconsistent (a real signal, keep it and raise repeat). Read the saved payloads for the three collapsed runs before deciding -- do not 'fix' a case that is correctly reporting a hard problem.

NOTE: collapseFloor 0.3 is working exactly as designed here -- ok=2/5, quality=0.934+/-0.039 -- so it separates the two modes cleanly and does NOT need re-fitting on this evidence.
close_reason: Workstreams 1-2 of docs/specs/eval-name-licensing.spec.md merged in PR #357: university-enrollment licenses CourseOffering/Offering, both check families resolve through the licence, suite bumped to 2.1.0. WS3 (alias-recording prompt compliance) stays open in the spec as provisional.

title: elementCount is recorded on CaseScore but nothing consumes it, so the denominator-inflation tripwire is unwired
description:
eval-split-stratification.spec.md names the risk that rating penalties leaves volume unpunished: a model inventing forty elements, half defective, now scores like one inventing four with two defects. The stated guard is that `elementCount` is recorded on CaseScore, so 'an arm inflating its denominator is visible in the record', with the tripwire 'if a candidate's mean elementCount rises materially and its score rises with it, the denominator is being gamed'.

The field exists. Nothing reads it. The one place that compares two arms is the optimizer's MetricLog, and `CaseScore.from_json` (optimizer/barwise_optimizer/barwise_cli.py:164) does not carry it -- explicit .get() lookups, so no break, just silence. The delta report has no denominator column.

The guard was specified, the field was added, and the consumer was never built. Same shape as the defects both eval specs were written to fix.

Fix: carry elementCount through CaseScore.from_json into MetricLog, report mean elementCount per arm in render_delta_report, and say so when it moves with the score.

title: resolveArtifact does not rank a narrower modelPrefix above a broader one, and its error tells the operator to do what they already did
description:
`specificity()` scores which match FIELDS are present -- provider 1, modelPrefix 2 -- and never how specific a prefix is. So a variant matching `claude-haiku-4-5-2026` ties with one matching `claude-haiku`, and the pair is refused:

  Error: Ambiguous prompt artifacts ... version haiku45-2 (modelPrefix=claude-haiku); version local-narrow-1 (modelPrefix=claude-haiku-4-5-2026). Narrow the match blocks so exactly one variant wins.

The advice is the one thing an operator in this position has already done. This is the first shape anyone testing a per-release variant against a shipped one will hit, and --artifacts exists precisely for that workflow.

Found while writing tests for barwise-850/851; asserted in packages/cli/tests/workspace/promptArtifacts.test.ts as documented-not-endorsed so it is not rediscovered.

Fix options: rank by matched prefix LENGTH so the narrower wins (a longer prefix is strictly more specific and the tie is artificial); or leave the tie and rewrite the message to name the real remedy. The first is recommended -- the tie is not a question an operator can meaningfully answer.

title: The review surface is artifact-driven but only half-reachable from the CLI
description:
Found auditing PR #338 for the defect it was fixing. barwise-847 wired reviewModel to the artifact seam; the CLI has caught up in one place and not the others.

FIXED in #338: `prompt artifact --surface review` refused with 'extraction only'. The one command whose job is 'which prompt would this configuration send' could not answer for the surface that had just started having an answer. Note that an EXISTING TEST asserted the refusal was correct -- the gap was locked in by a passing test, which is worth remembering as a shape.

STILL OPEN, both the same shape:

1. `prompt schema --surface review` refuses with 'no schema export yet (extraction only)'. buildReviewResponseSchema is private to reviewModel.ts and not exported from @barwise/llm. barwise-848 needs it -- scoreReview grades a payload against that schema's shape -- so export it and wire the command.

2. `barwise review` has no `--artifacts` and never reports which artifact it used. Extraction can be pointed at a candidate directory and says what it resolved; review can do neither, so there is no way to try a review variant without editing packages/llm/prompts/ and rebuilding, and no way to tell from the output which prompt produced a given review.

Both are small. Filed rather than folded into #338 because (2) overlaps the review-eval workstreams (barwise-848/849), which will want the same override to gate a candidate.
close_reason: Item 1 shipped: buildReviewResponseSchema exported and prompt schema --surface review wired. Item 2 resolved differently than filed (artifact-resolution-parity.spec.md, option 2): production commands deliberately gain no --artifacts; barwise prompt run --surface review --artifacts sends a candidate once, and runs record promptHash so the artifact used is recoverable

title: parseExtractionFromJson has no production caller, so the reference-generation rule is a procedure nobody automates
description:
Exported from @barwise/llm, exercised only by tests/TranscriptProcessor.test.ts. Nothing in src anywhere calls it.

Not dead code -- a DOCUMENTED PROCESS WITH NO IMPLEMENTATION. packages/promptlab/CLAUDE.md states as a standing rule: 'References are generated, not hand-written. The seed references were produced by running the recorded payloads through parseExtractionFromJson and serializing -- they cannot drift from what the pipeline actually builds.' That rule is why the seven train references can be trusted, and nothing automates it, so the guarantee rests on whoever last did it by hand having done it right.

Live work, not archaeology: barwise-845 requires generating references for the three dev cases and that IS this procedure. Whoever picks it up either writes the script or does it by hand and leaves the next person in the same position.

Fix: a script (scripts/regen-references.mjs, following scripts/regen-tutorial.mjs) or a CLI subcommand that takes a recorded payload and writes the .reference.orm.yaml. Then the standing rule has an implementation and a drift test can assert the references match what the pipeline builds today.
notes:

title: Review the test suite for tests that assert the wrong behaviour is correct
description:
Requested 2026-08-25. A new audit axis, and the one the unwired-capability sweep is least able to close.

PR #338 fixed `prompt artifact` refusing --surface review, wrong since barwise-847 made review artifact-driven. The gap survived a green suite because a test ASSERTED THE REFUSAL WAS CORRECT:

  it('rejects a surface it cannot print', ...)
    expect(stderr).toContain('extraction only');

That is worse than an untested gap. An untested gap is invisible; this one was visible, described, and pinned as a requirement, so any reviewer reading it would conclude the behaviour was intended.

WHAT WORKS (tried in the 2026-08-25 audit): grep expected error strings for 'yet', 'only', 'not supported', 'unsupported'. 'Yet' is the strongest tell -- it means temporary, and a test pinning a temporary state is the shape. Four hits, one real (prompt schema --surface review, barwise-855). THE DISCRIMINATOR is whether src PRODUCES the string or the test SUPPLIES it: three of four hits were the test feeding its own fixture text.

WHAT THAT MISSES, and why this needs a real pass rather than a grep: it only catches tests pinning an ERROR. It cannot catch a test pinning a wrong VALUE, a wrong fallback, or an assertion that passes for the wrong reason. barwise-840 was the second kind -- mutating CaseScore.floored to always return false was caught by NOTHING, because the report tests supplied the count as a literal and so asserted the consumer and never the computation.

Method for the real pass: sample-mutate the PRODUCER of any value a test feeds in by hand, and audit every test whose name begins 'rejects', 'refuses', 'throws' or 'does not' for whether the refusal is a requirement or a limitation. Prioritise packages where a capability seam exists: llm (artifacts, surfaces), cli (commands, flags), promptlab (scorer), core (format registry).

title: prompt eval/artifact need an --artifact-version flag; the default is reachable only by a shadow-directory trick
description: docs/local-eval-runbook.md's 'Gap worth closing', now tracked. prompt eval has no way to say 'this model, the default prompt': with builtins always in the candidate set, forcing the default while holding the model fixed requires shadowing the builtins with match-less copies (the runbook's /tmp/default-only recipe). An operator who does not know the trick will compare default vs variant by changing the model, confounding exactly what the comparison separates. Add --artifact-version <version|default> to prompt eval and prompt artifact, resolving within the candidate set and erroring on an unknown version. Wanted before the split-spec WS4 re-baseline, which runs the default arm on both models.

title: Extraction schema cannot express a disjunctive mandatory across fact types
description: InferredConstraint names one fact_type and roles within it, so the settled incident-response rule 'an incident has an alert, or a customer report, or both, and never neither' has no encoding: it spans roles in 'Incident originates from Alert' and 'Incident originates from Ticket'. The recorded haiku45-2 payload attempted it anyway, as a disjunctive_mandatory with one role plus the subset fields carrying the other fact type, and conformance rightly dropped that as arity_mismatch -- so the answer key pins the miss as a penalty (see scoreExtraction.test.ts, incident-response row). Core's constraint model does support cross-fact-type disjunctive mandatories; closing this needs a schema shape for them, parser support, and a conformance mirror. Until then the rule stays prompt-headroom evidence, recorded in the incident-response.eval.yaml comment.
